html:
MARKET OVERVIEW
🌎 The week "space" stopped being one trade.

Track every space stock live at Orbit Alpha

The week built toward a single moment, and that moment broke the basket. SpaceX priced its IPO at $135 per share for 555.6 million shares on Thursday night, in line with terms confirmed the previous week, and made its Nasdaq debut Friday under SPCX. Shares opened at $150, an 11% premium to the offer price, and closed up roughly 19% on the day at $160.95, with an intraday high of $176.52, putting the market cap near $2.2 trillion. MSCI index inclusion begins 13 June. The broader market absorbed the largest IPO in history without strain: the S&P 500 closed the week at 7,431.46 (+0.50% on the day), the Nasdaq Composite at 25,888.84 (+0.31%), and the Dow at 51,202.26 (+0.70%).

The first four days of the week extended the pre-IPO rally that has defined the sector since late May, with three independent developments layered on top, each worth tracking on its own terms. On Tuesday 9 June, Redwire entered into a new $500 million equity distribution agreement, terminating its May 2026 at-the-market programme and replacing it with an expanded facility, a second consecutive month of capital-raising activity for the name. On Thursday 11 June, Rocket Lab announced its addition to the Nasdaq-100 Index, effective before market open on Monday 22 June, alongside Astera Labs, CoreWeave, Nebius and Teradyne, RKLB jumped roughly 9% on the announcement alone. And on Wednesday 10 June, MDA Space's IPO-related lock-up agreement expired, releasing pre-listing shares for sale for the first time since its NYSE listing.

Then Friday arrived, and the trade inverted. The moment SPCX began trading, capital that had been parked in listed proxies, the closest available exposure to SpaceX for the past 18 months, rotated directly into the real thing. The reversal was sharp and broad: Virgin Galactic fell over 37%, Firefly dropped more than 20%, AST SpaceMobile fell over 16%, Redwire dropped more than 13% (compounding the dilution overhang from its ATM news two days earlier), Intuitive Machines fell around 12%, MDA fell roughly 9% (landing in the same week as its lock-up expiry), Spire fell roughly 8%, Rocket Lab fell 8-11%, and Planet Labs gave back roughly 9-16% depending on the measurement window. The Procure Space ETF dropped nearly 7% on the day.

SPACEX (SPCX)

SpaceX made its trading debut on Nasdaq Friday 12 June, pricing the IPO at $135 per share for 555.6 million shares Thursday night. Shares opened at $150 and closed up roughly 19% at $160.95, an intraday high of $176.52, putting the market cap near $2.2 trillion. MSCI index inclusion begins 13 June. For 18 months, listed space names have traded as proxies for an asset investors couldn't directly own. That constraint is now gone, and the debut absorbed the bulk of sector capital flows this week, the direct mechanism behind Friday's broad reversal across every other name on this list. The structural questions remain unchanged but now trade against a live tape: S&P 500 exclusion until at least mid-2027, a sub-5% float, and a 90-180 day lockup that concentrates a very large supply event into a thin market.

ROCKET LAB (RKLB)

On Thursday 11 June, Rocket Lab announced it will join the Nasdaq-100 Index, effective before market open on Monday 22 June, as part of the quarterly rebalancing alongside Astera Labs, CoreWeave, Nebius and Teradyne. The stock jumped roughly 9% on the announcement. This is a genuinely independent catalyst with its own mechanical driver, passive funds tracking over $800 billion in AUM will need to acquire the stock ahead of 22 June, regardless of sentiment elsewhere in the sector. RKLB still sold off with the rest of the group on Friday's SPCX-driven rotation, but the index flow is calendar-locked and arrives next week irrespective of where SPCX settles.

VIASAT (VSAT)

On 11 June, Viasat was awarded a prime contract by the US Space Force's Space Systems Command for the Protected Tactical SATCOM-Global (PTS-G) programme, covering the build, launch and delivery of the first in a planned fleet of small, maneuverable GEO satellites. The award is a follow-on to a 2025 system-design phase (Delivery Order 1) and adds to a string of defence wins this quarter, alongside the NOAA Hurricane Hunter contract from early June. Viasat's government SATCOM pipeline is converting at a steady cadence independent of the sector's SpaceX-driven moves, the kind of recurring, non-discretionary defence revenue that should anchor the multiple regardless of where the rest of the sector trades.

BLACKSKY TECHNOLOGY (BKSY)

BlackSky was awarded an NRO contract modification on 9 June to accelerate development of AROS as a commercial alternative for foundation imaging, its second piece of positive contract news in as many weeks following a multi-year automation renewal in late May. The recurring nature of NRO award flow gives BKSY one of the more defensible standalone narratives in the group, government Earth observation demand that has nothing to do with where capital is rotating on any given Friday.

SPIRE GLOBAL (SPIR)

On 10 June, Spire signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Diehl Defence at the ILA Berlin Airshow, targeting joint development of satellite-based early warning systems against ballistic and hypersonic missile threats. This is Spire's second European defence MoU in as many months, following the Schaeffler partnership, and reinforces a clear strategic pivot toward sovereign European space-security spending. The stock fell roughly 8% on the week despite the announcement, a reminder that even names with genuine positive catalysts weren't immune to Friday's sector-wide unwind.

REDWIRE (RDW)

On 9 June, Redwire entered into a new $500 million equity distribution agreement covering at-the-market sales, block trades and privately negotiated transactions, simultaneously terminating its May 2026 ATM programme without penalty. Proceeds are earmarked for working capital, potential debt repayment, acquisitions and R&D. This is the second consecutive month RDW has gone to the market for capital, and the timing, two days before the SPCX-driven sector reversal, meant the stock absorbed both a fresh dilution overhang and Friday's rotation in the same week, contributing to a decline of over 13%. Investors should watch whether the expanded facility gets drawn down quickly or held in reserve; the size relative to RDW's market cap is meaningful.

MDA SPACE (MDA)

MDA's IPO-related lock-up agreement expired on 10 June, freeing pre-listing shareholders to sell into the market for the first time since the company's NYSE listing earlier this year. The stock fell roughly 9% this week. As with Redwire, the lock-up expiry and Friday's SPCX rotation landed in the same window, making it difficult to isolate how much of the move was unlock-driven supply versus sector beta. The read-through for the rest of the portfolio: investors holding names with known unlock dates elsewhere in the sector should be alert to the risk of these events compounding with broader repricing moves rather than occurring in isolation.

MOMENTUS (MNTS)

On 12 June, Momentus announced a $25 million registered direct offering, 1,851,852 shares priced at-the-market under Nasdaq rules, with closing expected around 15 June, under a Form S-3 shelf that became effective 4 June. The stock fell sharply on the news, the second capital raise from MNTS in as many weeks. Management is using an elevated multiple to raise cash while it can; investors should treat this as the cleanest illustration in the sector of valuation running well ahead of the underlying revenue base.

Takeaway: Beneath the SPCX headline, the more durable story this week is supply. Three separate mechanisms put fresh share count into the market in the same five-day window: Redwire's new $500 million ATM on Tuesday, its second consecutive month of equity issuance; MDA's IPO lock-up expiry on Wednesday, releasing pre-listing holders for the first time; and Momentus's $25 million raise on Friday, its second in two weeks. None of these are forced sellers, they're management and early investors choosing to issue or sell into a market that has been running hot on SpaceX-adjacent enthusiasm since late May. That's a rational response to elevated valuations, but it's also a signal: when multiple insiders and issuers across a sector reach for the market in the same week, it's often a read on where they think relative value sits, and it rarely happens at the bottom. Friday's SPCX-driven rotation gave the sector a fundamental reason to sell, but the issuance pattern suggests some of this repricing was coming regardless, the IPO was the trigger, not the only cause. For the regime-change thesis: the names with calendar-locked, SPCX-independent catalysts, RKLB's Nasdaq-100 inclusion on 22 June, BKSY's NRO award, VSAT's Space Force contract, are the cleanest test of dispersion. But the issuance cluster is the other half of the picture, and it argues for some caution before reading Friday's selloff purely as a SpaceX-rotation story.

SENTIMENT SIGNAL
🎯 SPCX WEEK ONE: THE NUMBERS BEHIND THE NUMBERS

Friday's headline writes itself: $135.00 to $160.95, a 19.2% first-day pop, a $2.1-2.2 trillion market cap, and Elon Musk crossing the trillion-dollar personal net worth threshold on paper. But the headline figure is the least useful number from this week. Underneath it sits a deal structure, a shareholder map, and a set of forward estimates that tell you far more about how SPCX is likely to trade over the next six to twelve months than the first-day pop does. This deep dive goes underneath.

The demand picture: oversubscribed, but not as extreme as the price action suggests

By the time order books closed on Wednesday 10 June, the offering was reported as more than four times oversubscribed against the $75 billion target, with multiple institutional investors each placing orders north of $10 billion. Retail demand alone reportedly exceeded $100 billion. Total demand across institutional and retail was estimated around $150 billion, roughly double the deal size.

Here's the number that matters for positioning: a ~4x oversubscription on a $75 billion deal is enormous in absolute terms, but it's not actually an extreme ratio by IPO standards, smaller deals have produced oversubscription multiples an order of magnitude higher (Snowflake's 2020 IPO was reportedly oversubscribed over 100x). The practical read-through is that there's a large pool of disappointed institutional and retail buyers who didn't get the allocation they wanted, and that pool is a structural source of buying pressure in the early days, exactly the dynamic that helped produce Friday's 30%+ intraday spike before the stock settled to close up 19.2%. But it also means the "everyone who wants in is already in" thesis is wrong; there's real unmet demand still sitting on the sidelines, which cuts both ways, it's support on dips, but it's also a population of buyers who may have been burned by the intraday volatility and could turn cautious.

Who actually owns this thing, and who controls it

The S-1 shareholder disclosures give us the clearest picture yet of SpaceX's ownership structure, and it's worth understanding because it directly drives the float and lockup dynamics that will dominate trading for the next six months.

Musk's stake, valued at roughly $1 trillion on the IPO price, is reported to be worth up to five times the value of all shares sold in the entire IPO combined. That's the float problem in one sentence: the founder's personal stake alone dwarfs the entire public float several times over.

Below Musk, the largest individual shareholder is board member Antonio Gracias, holding more than 503 million Class A shares, roughly a 7.3% stake. Class B super-voting shares, the mechanism that preserves Musk's control regardless of equity dilution, are held by an extremely small group: Musk himself, COO Gwynne Shotwell, and Ira Ehrenpreis of DBL Partners (564,650 Class B shares plus 809,050 Class A). Major pre-IPO institutional holders include Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, Sequoia Capital, Valor Equity Partners, Thrive Capital, Alphabet, Baillie Gifford, D1 Capital Partners, and Fidelity, among others, though the S-1 doesn't break out their individual stakes with full granularity.

The takeaway for investors: this is a company where voting control is mathematically locked in regardless of how the stock trades, dilution from future raises, employee equity programmes, or even Musk's own eventual share sales (within the lockup framework below) will not threaten control. That's relevant to how you think about governance risk, and it's also part of why Senator Elizabeth Warren's letter requesting an SEC delay over governance concerns was always unlikely to change the timeline; the structure was disclosed and the deal proceeded as planned.

The lockup structure is the single most important mechanical fact about this stock for the next six months

Most IPOs use a simple 180-day lockup: insiders can't sell anything until day 180, then a wall of supply hits at once. SPCX did something structurally different, and every investor in the listed space sector needs to understand this schedule, because it will be the dominant technical driver of SPCX's price action (and by extension, sentiment toward the rest of the sector) through mid-December.

The schedule, as disclosed in the S-1:

  • After Q2 2026 earnings (expected mid-July to September): insiders can sell up to 20% of eligible locked-up shares, the first release.
  • Performance-triggered early release: if SPCX trades at least 30% above the $135 IPO price (i.e., $175.50+) for 5 of any 10 consecutive trading days before that first earnings release, an additional 10% of shares becomes eligible early. Worth noting, Friday's intraday high of $176.52 already touched this threshold on day one, though a single intraday print doesn't satisfy the "5 of 10 consecutive days" condition.
  • Five staggered time-based releases of up to 7% each, at 70, 90, 105, 120, and 135 days post-IPO, landing across roughly August through October.
  • After Q3 2026 earnings (mid-October to December): a further 28% release, the largest single tranche and explicitly flagged by multiple analysts as the most consequential supply event before the final unlock.
  • Day 180 (mid-December 2026): all remaining standard-lockup restrictions lift.

Musk himself sits entirely outside this structure. He and select major backers have committed to a full 366-day lockup, roughly June 2027, and Musk cannot participate in any of the early-release provisions.

Why this matters strategically: the staggered design is deliberate financial engineering. A traditional single-date lockup creates a predictable, calendar-visible cliff that the market prices in advance, often producing exactly the selling pressure it's trying to avoid, as everyone races to exit before everyone else. SpaceX's rolling structure spreads that supply across roughly five months, smaller, more digestible tranches rather than one event. It also has a second-order effect that matters for the sector: by increasing the tradeable float incrementally rather than all at once, it accelerates SPCX's qualification for major index inclusion (Nasdaq-100, and eventually S&P 500 once profitability conditions are met), which brings forced passive buying into a market that's simultaneously absorbing new insider supply. The two flows, more float available to sell, more passive demand arriving, are designed to roughly offset each other. Whether they actually do in practice is the single biggest technical question for SPCX (and the broader sector) over the second half of 2026.

For listed proxies, the practical implication: the 28% post-Q3-earnings release (likely landing October/November) is the date to have circled. If Friday's rotation out of RKLB, ASTS, LUNR et al. into SPCX was driven partly by SPCX's scarcity (low float, high demand), a meaningful float increase in Q4 could either ease that scarcity premium, or, if absorbed cleanly by index-driven demand, do nothing at all. Either way, it's a date worth tracking on the Orbit Alpha launch/events calendar going forward.

Nobody else is building this

The first formal sell-side coverage came from Oppenheimer's Timothy Horan on 11 June (notably, Oppenheimer was outside the underwriting syndicate, making this one of the more independent reads available), initiating at Outperform with a $190 price target, implying roughly 41% upside from the IPO price and a path to a ~$2.5 trillion valuation within 12-18 months. Horan's thesis is structural rather than financial: SpaceX is, in his framing, the only vertically-integrated entity combining the capital, data, large language models, hardware manufacturing, and engineering talent to build AI infrastructure in space, and he argues orbital data centres could ultimately be more cost-effective than terrestrial ones.

The broader sell-side consensus, as of this week, sits at a $164 average 12-month target across five analysts (four Buy, one Sell), with a $227 high and a $63 low, an unusually wide dispersion that itself tells you something: this is a stock where reasonable, informed analysts disagree by a factor of more than 3.5x on fair value. That's not normal for a company this large, and it reflects genuine uncertainty about which of SpaceX's three segments should set the multiple.

The capex math doesn't work without a miracle

The most substantive bear case came from Steve Eisman, the investor whose subprime short was chronicled in "The Big Short," who told CNBC ahead of pricing that he had "no interest" in either direction, not long, not short, on a $1.75 trillion valuation. His reasoning is worth taking seriously because it's not a sentiment argument, it's a capital-intensity argument: Eisman cited SpaceX's capex at 42% of revenue in fiscal 2023, climbing to 215% of revenue in the most recent quarter (Q1 2026). A company spending more than double its revenue on capex every quarter is not behaving like the satellite-internet-and-launch business the bulls are valuing it as, it's behaving like an AI infrastructure buildout, and AI infrastructure buildouts are judged on a completely different, much less forgiving, set of metrics.

That framing is reinforced by Goldman Sachs' own modelling, reported this week: Goldman projects SPCX will run a negative free cash flow of $105 billion in 2029. For context, that single year's projected cash burn is larger than the entire previous IPO record (Saudi Aramco's $25.6 billion raise in 2019), four times over. Whether or not you think the AI infrastructure bet pays off, $105 billion of negative FCF in a single year is the kind of number that should be sitting in every investor's head when SPCX trades at 109-116x trailing revenue.

This is now an AI infrastructure stock that happens to also do satellites and rockets

Every piece of this week's news points the same direction. The valuation dispersion ($63-$227), the capex ratio (215% of revenue), the FCF projection (-$105bn in 2029), the bull case (orbital AI data centres), they're all about the AI segment, not Starlink or Falcon/Starship. Starlink is the part of this company every analyst can underwrite with confidence (profitable, growing, understood). Falcon/Starship is a known quantity (expensive, strategically essential, not a near-term profit driver). The entire valuation argument, in both directions, is actually an argument about whether xAI's orbital compute thesis is real, and at what cost.

What this means for the rest of your portfolio

  1. The performance-trigger lockup clause (30% above IPO price for 5 of 10 days) is now a live tripwire. SPCX touched $176.52 intraday on day one, just above the $175.50 trigger. If it holds above that level into next week, an additional 10% of insider shares becomes eligible for early sale ahead of Q2 earnings, a supply event that could arrive far sooner than the market currently expects. Worth monitoring daily.
  2. The proxy trade isn't dead, but it's now conditional. Friday's rotation showed that when SPCX is the marginal trade, listed proxies lose, hard. But SPCX's float is still thin and its lockup-driven supply increases are staged and predictable. Between now and the next major float-increase event (likely the post-Q3-earnings 28% release), there may be windows where SPCX's own supply constraints reassert themselves and capital flows back toward proxies, particularly ones with their own catalysts (RKLB's Nasdaq-100 inclusion, ASTS's BlueBird launch).
  3. The wide analyst dispersion is itself useful information. A $63-$227 target range means the market hasn't agreed on a valuation framework yet. Until it does, expect SPCX to remain one of the most volatile large-cap names on the Nasdaq, which means its correlation with the listed proxies (in both directions) is likely to stay elevated and unstable. Don't assume Friday's rotation pattern repeats identically next time SPCX moves sharply, it could just as easily reverse.

Takeaway: Strip away the bell-ringing ceremony and the trillion-dollar headlines, and Issue #9's central fact is this: SPCX's first trading day didn't resolve the valuation debate, it just moved it onto a liquid, continuously-priced instrument with a known, staged supply schedule. The 19.2% first-day pop tells you demand exceeded the (thin) available float. It tells you almost nothing about whether $160.95, or $135, or $227, is the right price for a company spending 215% of revenue on capex while promising orbital AI infrastructure. That debate is now live, public, and will be re-litigated at every lockup tranche between now and mid-December. The performance trigger at $175.50 is the first checkpoint, and it's arriving within days, not months.
